name: Acorns Design System
summary: Rebuild Acorns' friendly micro-investing look: Oak purple + Acorn Green, a signature allocation donut, and a gradient Round-Ups card.
description: Rebuild Acorns' friendly micro-investing look: Oak purple + Acorn Green, a signature allocation donut, and a gradient Round-Ups card that make small, automatic investing feel warm rather than clinical.

whatYouGet: A SwiftUI Color/Font token set covering Acorns' dual-brand purple-and-green palette, the fixed six-slice allocation-chart palette, and a Nunito Sans weight ladder with tabular figures baked in
Full component specs for the two screens that define Acorns: the animated allocation donut with center label + legend, and the gradient Round-Ups spare-change card
Motion, haptic, dark-mode, and accessibility notes so a rebuilt Invest dashboard sweeps in, counts up, and reads correctly to VoiceOver
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer who specializes in recreating best-in-class consumer fintech design systems with pixel-accurate tokens, faithful motion, and production-ready component code. You have deep experience translating a brand's emotional intent (in this case: micro-investing that feels encouraging rather than intimidating) into concrete SwiftUI view hierarchies.
</role>

<reference_data>
Acorns runs on two brand colors with distinct jobs, never interchanged: Acorn Green #6FBF4E is the action/growth color (primary CTAs, gains, the active tab), and Acorns Oak #5A2B82 is the trust/brand color (the Round-Ups card, secondary buttons, structural headers). Supporting tones: Green Bright #84D962 (dark-mode positive), Green Pressed #5AA53D, Oak Bright #7B43A8 (top of the Round-Ups gradient), Oak Pressed #47206A, Oak Soft #C8AEDF (dark-mode outline/glyph tint). Canvas is a warm lilac-white #F5F3F8 in light mode and a deep aubergine #14121A in dark mode — never pure white or pure black. Surfaces step to #FFFFFF (light) / #1E1B27 and #292533 (dark). Text runs #1F1A2B / #6E6480 / #9C92AD in light and #F2EFF6 / #ADA4BC / #756B85 in dark. The fixed allocation-chart palette is Oak #5A2B82 (Large Company), Green #6FBF4E (Small Company), Teal #45C2B0 (International), Gold #F2C84B (Real Estate/REIT), Coral #F2785C (Bonds), Lilac #9B6FD4 (Emerging Markets) — this mapping never changes between screens or themes.
Typeface: a rounded geometric humanist sans; Nunito Sans (SIL OFL) is the correct free substitute, run at heavy weights (800-900) for headline numbers and titles, with tabular figures enabled on every currency value. Hierarchy runs from a 38pt weight-900 portfolio total down through 22pt/18pt section and card titles to 12pt weight-700 uppercased eyebrow labels with +0.4pt tracking.
Distinctive UI patterns: (1) the Allocation Donut, a ~168pt conic ring with a canvas-colored center hole showing the portfolio-style label plus "100% invested", segments sweeping in clockwise on load; (2) the Round-Ups card, an 18pt-radius Oak-gradient (#5A2B82 to #7B43A8) panel showing accumulated spare change and the $5 auto-invest threshold; (3) the Found Money/Earn feed, brand-chip rows with green "+$" cashback amounts that auto-invest; (4) the portfolio-total-plus-all-time-gain header, a big tabular number with a green triangle delta beneath it; (5) full-pill (500pt radius) buttons everywhere, green for primary action and Oak purple for secondary/brand; (6) a gentle upward growth-projection chart with soft green area fill.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never let green and purple swap jobs — green is only for action/growth/gains, Oak purple is only for brand/structure/secondary actions. Mixing them erases the dual-brand identity that makes Acorns legible at a glance.
2. Use dark forest ink (#14302A), never white, for text sitting directly on Acorn Green — the bright green fails contrast with white text, and this is one of the most-repeated rules in the source system.
3. Dark mode is deep aubergine (#14121A), not pure black, and light mode is warm lilac-white (#F5F3F8), not pure white — both are tinted from the Oak brand hue, and using neutral black/white flattens the personality.
4. The allocation donut and Round-Ups card must stay fully saturated in dark mode — only chrome (dividers, secondary text) should recede; desaturating the data visualization breaks the "growth is always visible" promise.
5. Enable tabular/monospaced digits on every currency figure — portfolio total, legend values, deltas — so numbers never jitter or misalign as they update.
6. Keep buttons at full pill radius (500pt) always; a squared-off button reads as generic fintech rather than Acorns' rounded, approachable voice.
7. Reserve heavy drop shadows for cards and sheets only — never put a shadow on the donut or on legend/feed rows, which are separated by hairline dividers instead; this keeps the calm, flat surface the brand relies on.
8. Animate meaningfully, not decoratively: the donut sweeps clockwise from 12 o'clock on load (~600ms ease-out), the portfolio number counts up digit-by-digit on change, and milestones trigger a leaf/confetti burst — motion should always read as "growth happening," never generic bounce.
9. Keep copy plain-English and motivational in any placeholder text you generate (e.g. "Small amounts add up") — Acorns' voice is a real, distinctive part of the system, not filler.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Sprout — round-up micro-investing for students"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Invest dashboard, allocation detail, Round-Ups settings, Found Money feed, onboarding]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly — if adapting, note which elements must change vs. stay]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must use client's own logo/name; may reuse Acorns' purple+green formula or must invent a new pairing]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17+, using .sensoryFeedback and .contentTransition(.numericText())]
- Dark mode requirement: [full parity required / nice-to-have / not needed]
- Data model available: [e.g. do you have real allocation percentages, Round-Ups totals, and cashback partner data, or should placeholders be used?]
- Any deviations from source: [e.g. different asset classes, no cashback partner program, different portfolio-style naming]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file with every token above named and commented with its hex/role, plus a `.acornTabular()` view modifier for tabular figures.
2. Full component code for the Allocation Donut + Legend (animated conic-ring sweep, center label, tap-to-highlight-and-scroll-to-legend interaction) and the Round-Ups gradient card.
3. The portfolio header component (big tabular total + green delta triangle + range-switch tap target) and the Found Money/Earn feed row.
4. Pill-button components (primary green, secondary Oak, outline, text) with correct pressed/disabled states.
5. Motion and haptic notes: donut sweep timing, number-ticker count-up, milestone celebration, card-press scale, with Reduce Motion fallbacks specified for each.
6. A dark-mode variant of every component above, explicitly calling out which elements must stay fully saturated (donut, Round-Ups gradient, Found Money green) vs. which recede (dividers, secondary text).
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver labels for the portfolio header, donut (combined summary + per-slice legend), and Found Money rows; Dynamic Type behavior per component; and confirmation that green/dark-forest-ink text pairs pass WCAG AA.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Apple Wallet Design System
summary: Recreate Apple Wallet's true-black stage: a vertically stacked, physically animated card deck with the titanium Apple Card as centerpiece.
description: Recreate Apple Wallet's true-black stage: a vertically stacked, physically animated card deck with the titanium Apple Card as centerpiece, using nothing but a title, a stack, and issuer-owned card faces.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Wallet's true-black canvas, the Apple Card titanium gradient, and the SF Pro Display/Text size-based switchover rule
A working card-stack component (matchedGeometryEffect-based expand/collapse, 80pt peek interval, spring physics) plus the Apple Card face and a generic issuer card face
Detail-sheet, transaction-row, and Apple Pay-invocation specs with motion, haptic, and accessibility notes for a card-based payments app
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer specializing in recreating Apple's own first-party interaction physics and HIG-compliant chrome, with particular expertise in matchedGeometryEffect-driven card stacks, spring animation tuning, and building interfaces that get out of the way of the content they hold.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is true black #000000 (never the system dark-mode gray #1C1C1E) — the whole point is that the void makes cards look like floating physical objects. Surfaces: #1C1C1E (Surface 1, expanded-card detail panels), #2C2C2E (Surface 2, pressed states), a glass overlay rgba(255,255,255,0.12) for the "+" button and toolbar buttons, and a #262629 hairline divider. Apple Card specifics: titanium gradient 135° from #E8E8EB (highlight) through #A8A8AD (midtone) to #3D3D3F (shadow), a white Apple-logo glyph, a #C7AC73 gold chip glyph, and a #FF3B30 red Daily Cash circle. Text: pure white #FFFFFF primary, #A0A0A5 secondary, #636368 tertiary; system blue #0A84FF for links; #30D158 success, #FF9F0A warning, #FF453A error.
Typography follows Apple's own documented rule: SF Pro Display for anything ≥20pt (the 34pt "Wallet" title, 28pt sheet titles), SF Pro Text for ≤17pt (body, action buttons, section headers). SF Mono is used ONLY for the masked card-number last-4 on a card face — nowhere else. Tabular figures are mandatory on every balance, transaction amount, and last-4.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Wallet: (1) the card stack itself — cards overlap with a fixed 80pt peek on a single vanishing-point-aligned column, never a grid; (2) card expand/collapse via a bouncy-but-contained spring (response 0.5, damping 0.8) with the rest of the stack tucking down in parallel; (3) the Apple Card's titanium gradient + subtle brushed-metal noise overlay as the signature object; (4) heavy, long dark shadows (rgba(0,0,0,0.5), 24pt blur) that only work because the canvas is true black; (5) a translucent action toolbar (.regularMaterial) with 44pt circular glass buttons at the base of an expanded card; (6) issuer-controlled card faces — Wallet supplies only the frame (10pt corner radius, fixed across every card type), never the typography or color inside a card.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never substitute #1C1C1E (or any dark gray) for the canvas — it must be literal #000000, because the entire floating-card illusion depends on true black, not a lighter "dark mode" gray.
2. Never grid or carousel the cards — always a single vertical column with vanishing-point alignment and a fixed 80pt peek; compressing the peek to "show more" breaks the rhythm that reads as a stack.
3. Keep every card's corner radius at exactly 10pt regardless of card type (credit card, boarding pass, transit pass) — Wallet's radius is a fixed constant, not a per-content choice.
4. Never theme or restyle a card's face from the app side — a card's internal typography, color, and logo belong entirely to the issuer (as if delivered via a manifest); the app only owns the frame, the stack physics, and the shadow.
5. Use heavy, long shadows (~0.5 opacity, 24-32pt blur) on every card — a soft, low-opacity shadow that reads fine on white becomes invisible on true black, so err heavy here specifically.
6. Reserve SF Mono strictly for the masked last-4 digits on a card face; body copy, labels, and buttons always use SF Pro Text/Display — mixing these breaks the documented type-switchover rule.
7. Never run a tab bar — Wallet has none, ever, and the card stack itself is the entire navigation model; adding tabs signals a misunderstanding of the reference.
8. Never expand two cards simultaneously — the stack-physics model assumes exactly one card is expanded at a time; anything else breaks the tuck-down animation contract.
9. Apply a 0.5pt inner top highlight (rgba(255,255,255,0.08)) to every card face in addition to its drop shadow — this is what sells the "paper-thin glass object" feel rather than a flat rectangle with a shadow.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Vaultline — a digital card wallet for a regional bank's card program"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. card stack home, expanded card detail with transactions, add-card flow, Apple Pay-style confirmation overlay]
- Card types to support: [e.g. just credit/debit, or also boarding passes / transit passes / loyalty cards]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must keep true-black canvas but substitute a different primary card design language]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17+ for .sensoryFeedback, Material, and matchedGeometryEffect]
- Number of cards expected in a typical user's stack: [affects whether search/filter is ever needed — Wallet deliberately omits it]
- Dark-mode-only or light/dark parity: [note that real Wallet stays dark regardless of system setting]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the true-black canvas, surface steps, Apple Card titanium gradient stops, and the SF Pro Display/Text switchover fonts with tabular-digit variants.
2. Full card-stack component code: the ZStack/ScrollView layout with 80pt peek offsets, matchedGeometryEffect-driven expand/collapse, and the spring animation parameters (response 0.5, damping 0.8) for expand and the reverse for collapse.
3. The Apple Card face component (titanium gradient, noise overlay, chip glyph, Daily Cash chip) and one generic issuer card face template showing how a different card's colors/logo slot in without touching the frame code.
4. The detail-sheet transaction row and grouped-list row components, plus the translucent action toolbar at the base of an expanded card.
5. Motion and haptic notes: exact spring/easing values for expand, collapse, drag-to-dismiss threshold and rubber-band resistance, and which haptic (`.impactOccurred` weight) fires at each interaction point.
6. A dark-mode note explicitly stating Wallet does not have a separate light theme — and how to structure the code so that's an intentional constant, not a missed color-scheme branch.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver labels for a card in collapsed vs. expanded state, Dynamic Type behavior (title/body scale, card-face typography stays fixed since it's treated as artwork), and a Reduce Motion fallback (linear cross-fade instead of spring bounce).
</what_to_give_me>

name: Binance Design System
summary: Build a dense, dark, trading-terminal UI with Binance's sans/mono type split, absolute green-up/red-down semantics, and a depth-shaded order book.
description: Build a dense, dark, trading-terminal UI with Binance's sans/mono type split, absolute green-up/red-down semantics, and a depth-shaded order book that packs a markets list without ever feeling cramped.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Binance's near-black terminal canvas, single yellow brand accent, and the mandatory sans-for-words/mono-for-numbers typographic split
Component specs for the two signature surfaces — the dense Markets list row with a colored percentage pill, and the depth-shaded Order Book with growing translucent bars
A Buy/Sell trade ticket, Convert card, and motion/haptic notes (including the price-tick flash) for a compact, data-dense exchange UI
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer who specializes in high-density financial trading interfaces — the kind of engineer who has shipped real-time order books, tick-flashing price cells, and terminal-grade list density without ever sacrificing 60fps scroll performance.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is near-black #0B0E11 (dark is the default and dominant mode, not an afterthought). Surface steps: #181A20 (Surface 1, cards/sheets/nav), #1E2026 (Surface 2, search fields, segmented controls), #2B3139 (Surface 3, pressed rows, chips, hairline dividers). The single brand accent is Binance Yellow #F0B90B (pressed #C99400, 12% tint #F0B90B1F) — used only for the primary CTA, active tab, active market-tab underline, and links; it never doubles as anything else. Market semantics are absolute and theme-invariant: Up/Buy/Bid Green #0ECB81 and Down/Sell/Ask Red #F6465D never invert between light and dark mode, because a trader's muscle memory depends on the mapping staying fixed. Light-mode canvas is #FFFFFF with #F5F5F5/#FAFAFA surfaces and #EAECEF dividers — accents (yellow, green, red) stay identical across both themes.
Typography is a strict sans/mono split: BinancePlex (IBM Plex Sans as the open fallback) for every word — titles, labels, tab names — and BinancePlex Mono (IBM Plex Mono fallback) with tabular figures for every number — balances, prices, the order book, percentages, volume. This split, not weight or size, is the primary signal that something is data. Weight is concentrated at 400/500/600/700 with no thin or black weights; color (not bold vs. regular) is what carries a value's positive/negative sign.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Binance: (1) the Markets List Row — coin icon, pair name + 24h volume stacked, monospace price + USD-equivalent stacked and right-aligned, and a solid colored percentage-change pill, all inside a dense 56pt row with 12pt padding; (2) the Order Book — asks above, bids below, a spread row between, each row backed by a translucent depth bar (rgba fill) that grows from the trailing edge proportional to cumulative size; (3) a price-cell flash — a cell briefly tints green or red at ~10% opacity for 150ms the instant its price ticks, described as "the heartbeat of the app"; (4) the Convert card — two stacked from/to tiles separated by a circular yellow swap button, ending in one full-width yellow confirm; (5) percentage-slider chips (25/50/75/100%) on the trade ticket; (6) tight radii throughout trading UI — 2pt depth bars, 4pt pills, 8pt buttons/inputs — never the 16pt+ radii consumer apps use.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never introduce a second saturated brand color — Binance Yellow #F0B90B is singular; if you need another accent for something, it almost certainly should be neutral gray or one of the fixed semantic greens/reds instead.
2. Put black/near-black text (#0B0E11) on yellow buttons, never white — this is explicitly called out because it's the opposite of most brand buttons and is easy to get backwards by habit.
3. Set every single number in monospace with tabular figures — prices, percentages, volumes, quantities, balances — with zero exceptions; a proportional-font price breaks column alignment across the whole markets list and order book.
4. Never invert up/down colors between light and dark mode, and never use green for a falling asset or red for a rising one under any circumstance — this mapping is load-bearing for a trader's reflexes.
5. Keep list rows dense (12pt vertical padding) rather than padding generously "to feel friendly" — density is Binance's actual product differentiator versus consumer fintech apps, not an oversight to fix.
6. Build depth/elevation from surface-tone steps (#0B0E11 → #181A20 → #1E2026 → #2B3139) plus 1pt borders, not drop shadows — shadows barely register on a near-black canvas and Binance relies on tone stepping instead, reserving actual shadow for floating sheets and the sticky trade ticket only.
7. Never animate the order book with springy/bouncy motion — reflow it with a flat ease-out (~120ms) because live trading data must read as stable and reliable, not playful.
8. Color alone must never carry the sign of a number — always pair a +/- prefix (and ideally an up/down arrow glyph) with the green/red color, since colorblind users need the redundant cue on financial data specifically.
9. Keep radii tight on anything trading-related (2-8pt) even when the rest of your app uses larger radii elsewhere — a 16pt+ corner on a markets row or order-book cell reads as a different, softer product than a terminal.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Ledgerline — a compact crypto/stock trading terminal for power users"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Markets list, Trade screen with chart + order book, Convert flow, Wallet/Funding overview]
- Asset classes: [e.g. crypto only, crypto + equities, futures/leverage support needed?]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must swap the single accent color from yellow to the client's own brand color while keeping the same density/semantics rules]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 16+ baseline, iOS 17+ for .sensoryFeedback]
- Real-time data source: [state whether you have a live price/order-book feed to wire up, or need mock/simulated tick data]
- Dark-mode-only or light/dark parity: [note Binance treats dark as default/primary, light as secondary]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the canvas/surface steps, the single yellow accent with its tint, the theme-invariant green/red semantics, and both the BinancePlex-style sans and mono font ladders with a `.bnTabular()` modifier.
2. Full component code for the Markets List Row (icon, stacked pair/volume, stacked price/USD, percentage pill) and the depth-shaded Order Book (ask/bid rows with proportional translucent bars, spread row with directional arrow).
3. The Buy/Sell Trade Ticket (segmented toggle, percentage-slider chips, submit button that swaps color/label with side) and the Convert card (swap-tile pair + circular swap button).
4. The price-tick-flash mechanism as a reusable view modifier or state pattern, with exact timing (150ms fade) and color logic.
5. Motion and haptic notes: tab-underline slide, Buy/Sell toggle color-morph, order-book reflow easing, Convert swap flip, and which haptic fires on order submit vs. percentage-chip snap vs. filled order.
6. A light-mode variant note confirming which tokens change (canvas, surfaces, text) and which stay theme-invariant (yellow, green, red) — light mode should never require a second logic branch for accents.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver phrasing for a markets row and an order-book row, the mandatory +/- and arrow-glyph pairing for colorblind users, Dynamic Type behavior (words scale, numeric/mono columns and tab labels stay fixed), and a Reduce Motion fallback for the price-flash and Convert-swap animations.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Cash App Design System
summary: Build Cash App's pop-art-club-flyer money app: near-black canvas, one violent Cash Green, a giant $-amount keypad, and a label-free icon-only tab bar.
description: Build Cash App's pop-art-club-flyer money app: near-black canvas, one violent Cash Green, a giant $-amount keypad, and a label-free icon-only tab bar that turns sending money into a cultural statement rather than a banking task.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Cash App's pure-black canvas, single Cash Green accent, and the Cash Sans / Cash Sans Mono weight ladder with black-weight (900) screen titles
The signature giant $-amount keypad component (auto-shrinking hero number, custom 3x4 keypad, glow-on-valid-amount) plus the matte-black Cash Card render and Activity row
An icon-only, no-label tab bar spec, plus motion/haptic notes for the Pay flow and dark-only-by-brand accessibility guidance
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer with a strong eye for brand-driven, culturally distinctive product design — the kind of engineer equally comfortable writing precise SwiftUI layout code and defending unconventional choices (icon-only tab bars, black text on a bright green button) that exist for real brand reasons rather than by accident.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is pure black #000000 — not a warm dark gray, not #111 — with Surface 1 #0F0F0F and Surface 2 #1A1A1A as the only "elevation" (fill-color contrast, never shadows). Dividers sit at #1F1F1F, barely visible by design. Cash Green #00D632 is the single brand accent (pressed #00B829, dim/disabled #008C20) — it touches only the Pay button, a valid-amount glow, success states, and the active tab glyph; Bitcoin Orange #F7931A is confined strictly to the Bitcoin tab/line, and Boost Red #FF453A only marks declines/losses. Text is pure white #FFFFFF primary (no off-white), #9E9E9E secondary, #6E6E6E tertiary, with a faint green-ghost #005C16 for the empty "$0" state.
Typography is Cash Sans (Inter as the open substitute) for words and Cash Sans Mono (JetBrains Mono substitute) for every dollar amount and every $Cashtag, always with tabular numerals. Screen titles ("Money", "Card", "Activity") are set in the heaviest available weight (900/Black) at 28pt — this single stylistic choice is one of the app's clearest signatures. Hero amounts on the keypad run up to 96pt weight 700 with tight negative tracking (-2pt), auto-shrinking as digits are added to stay on one line.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Cash App: (1) the $-Amount Keypad — the entire Pay tab is built around one enormous, auto-shrinking dollar figure over a custom 3x4 numeric keypad ("0" double-width), with the digits gaining a soft Cash Green text-glow the instant the amount becomes valid; (2) an icon-only bottom tab bar with absolutely no labels, ever, where the center Pay tab renders a distinct oversized "$" glyph as the visual anchor; (3) black text on the green Pay button (not white) as a deliberate, repeated brand rule; (4) the matte-black Cash Card render with the user's $Cashtag etched in a chosen accent color and explicitly no shadow; (5) randomly-assigned saturated avatar colors (pink, orange, blue, purple, green) for users without a photo, treated as part of the visual identity rather than a fallback to hide; (6) commissioned, intentionally imperfect hand-drawn Boost glyphs standing in for what would elsewhere be stock category icons.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Canvas must be literal #000000, never a warm dark gray like #111 — Cash App's flatness and contrast depend on true black, and a softened dark gray reads as a completely different, more generic dark-mode app.
2. Cash Green #00D632 is the ONLY accent color in the entire app — resist the urge to add a second brand color for variety; the whole point is that green means "money action" and appears nowhere else.
3. Put black text on the green Pay button, never white — this is the single most-repeated, most load-bearing contrast rule in the system and is easy to get backwards from habit with other brands' green buttons.
4. Never add shadows anywhere — depth exists only as fill-color steps (#000000 → #0F0F0F → #1A1A1A); a drop shadow anywhere in this UI is an immediate tell that the brief wasn't followed.
5. The bottom tab bar must be icon-only with zero labels, and inactive icons stay at full white opacity (never dimmed) — both are explicit, deliberate departures from standard iOS tab-bar conventions, not oversights to "fix."
6. Every dollar amount and every $Cashtag renders in the mono face with tabular numerals and keeps its "$" prefix — a Cashtag without its dollar sign, or an amount in a proportional font, breaks the brand's core visual vocabulary.
7. Reserve Bitcoin Orange strictly for the Bitcoin tab and BTC price line — do not let it bleed into other "crypto-adjacent" UI, since disciplined accent use is explicitly part of the brand's restraint.
8. Give the Pay screen's amount real room — reserve roughly the top 40% of the viewport for it alone; cramming other content above or beside the giant number undermines the "the number is the product" design intent.
9. Use randomly-assigned saturated colors for photo-less avatars and commissioned-feeling (not stock) icon art for Boosts — both are treated as intentional brand texture, so a generic gray-circle avatar or a standard SF Symbol in these two spots is a miss, not a neutral default.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Beam — a peer-to-peer payments app for a younger, culture-forward audience"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Pay keypad, Activity feed, Card tab with a branded card render, Money/balance tab]
- Card program: [does the app have its own debit-card product to render, or is this payments-only?]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must use the client's own single accent color instead of Cash Green while keeping the pure-black-canvas + no-shadow rules]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 16+, with iOS 17 sensoryFeedback for keypad taps]
- Cultural/illustration budget: [do you have or need commissioned illustration for Boost-style promotional glyphs, or should placeholders be used?]
- Light-mode requirement: [Cash App treats light mode as an accessibility fallback only — confirm if that's true here too]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the pure-black canvas/surface steps, the single Cash Green accent with its pressed/dim states, and the Cash-Sans-style sans/mono font ladder with a tabular-numerals modifier.
2. Full component code for the $-Amount Keypad screen: the auto-shrinking hero amount with conditional green glow, the custom 3x4 keypad grid (double-width "0"), and the twin Request/Pay button pair with correct black-on-green contrast.
3. The Cash Card render (matte-black, etched Cashtag in a chosen accent, no shadow) and the Activity Row (avatar, name/subtitle, green "+" or white "-" tabular amount).
4. The icon-only, no-label bottom tab bar with the oversized center Pay glyph and the full-white-opacity inactive-icon rule.
5. Motion and haptic notes: the keypad digit-drop spring, the Pay-button send sequence (scale + green flash + confirmation sheet), the Cash Card 3D flip, and which haptic (`.impactOccurred`/`.notificationOccurred`) fires at each step.
6. A light-mode note describing exactly what changes (canvas to white, text to black, green darkened slightly for AA) and confirming it is treated as an accessibility fallback rather than the brand's primary face.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver phrasing for an Activity row and the keypad amount, Dynamic Type behavior (most labels scale; the keypad hero amount is intentionally auto-sized and does not honor user text-size scaling), and a Reduce Motion fallback for the keypad spring and Boost-activation confetti.

name: Charles Schwab Design System
summary: Build Charles Schwab's calm brokerage UI: Schwab Navy + one cyan action color, a tabular-numeral accounts list, and the account-to-trade-ticket spine.
description: Build Charles Schwab's calm brokerage UI: Schwab Navy + one cyan action color, a tabular-numeral accounts list, and the account-to-trade-ticket spine that makes handling large sums feel steady rather than exciting.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Schwab's navy-and-cyan institutional palette, strict gain/loss-only semantic color rule, and a Source Sans 3 tabular-numeral type ramp
Component specs for the navy-gradient Total Value hero, the Account List Cell, and the centerpiece Trade Ticket (segmented Buy/Sell, tabular fields, estimated-cost card, Review/Place order flow)
Balances-tile and Positions-table specs plus motion/haptic notes tuned for calm, non-bouncy financial UI
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer specializing in institutional financial products — brokerage and banking apps where restraint, tabular alignment, and unambiguous color semantics matter more than visual flourish, and where a bug in gain/loss coloring is a trust-breaking defect, not a cosmetic one.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is white #FFFFFF (light) or a deep maritime navy #0A1622 (dark) — never pure black. Surfaces step to #F2F6F8/#E6EDF1 (light) and #11212F/#18303F (dark), with dividers at #DBE3E8 (light) and #1F3A4A (dark). The single action color is Schwab Blue #009DDC (pressed #0080B5), paired with Schwab Navy #003B5C for the hero gradient and secondary money-movement actions; a brightened Sky Accent (#0078A8 light / #46BEEC dark) covers links and selected-tab tints. Gain/loss color is strictly reserved for financial semantics — gain #16895F light / #18B07B dark, loss #C8443D light / #E2564E dark, flat uses secondary text color — and is never repurposed as a generic destructive-button or success-toast color elsewhere in the app.
Typography is a clean humanist sans (Source Sans 3, SIL OFL, as the free stand-in for Schwab's proprietary "Charles Modern"), with tabular/lining figures enabled on every monetary figure without exception — total value, balances, prices, quantities, percentages, estimated cost. Weight signals importance: total value and row balances sit at 800, labels at 400-600; the scale itself is compact (10pt to 34pt) because hierarchy comes from weight and tabular alignment, not dramatic size jumps.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Schwab: (1) the Account Hero — a navy gradient (#003B5C to #002A42) block carrying a 34pt tabular Total Value plus a day-change line with a triangle glyph, kept even in dark mode because the gradient itself carries brand identity; (2) the Account List Cell — a flat 66pt hairline row (never a card) with an icon chip, account name over masked number, and a right-aligned balance-over-percent-change pair; (3) the Trade Ticket as the visual centerpiece — an inset Buy/Sell segmented control, label-left/tabular-value-right field rows, an Estimated Cost row, and a sticky Review Order button leading to a read-only Review screen before Place Order; (4) a 2-column Balances Tiles grid (Cash available / Buying power / Market value / Day change); (5) dark navy text (#002233), not white, on the bright Schwab Blue button, because white fails contrast at body sizes on that specific blue.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never use white text on the Schwab Blue button — always dark navy #002233; the blue is bright enough that white-on-blue genuinely fails contrast at body text sizes, unlike most brand-blue buttons.
2. Reserve green/red strictly for gain/loss — never repurpose green for a generic "success" toast or red for a generic "destructive" button in a context that could be mistaken for a price move; in a brokerage app that ambiguity is a real trust problem, not a style nitpick.
3. Every monetary figure must use tabular/lining numerals with no exceptions — total value, balances, prices, quantities, percentages, and the trade ticket's estimated cost all need to align in a column; a single proportional-figure number breaks the whole list's alignment.
4. Use a deep maritime navy (#0A1622), never pure black, for the dark canvas — the navy tint is what keeps dark mode feeling like the same institutional brand rather than a generic OLED-black reskin.
5. Keep the account list as flat single-column hairline rows, never cards — reserve card chrome (12pt-radius surfaces) specifically for the hero, the trade ticket, balances tiles, and quote cards, so "card" reads as a meaningful visual signal rather than default styling.
6. Treat the trade ticket as the app's centerpiece, not a modal afterthought — its segmented Buy/Sell control, tabular right-aligned fields, and Estimated Cost card deserve the same design care as the Account Hero.
7. Never animate a changing balance by rolling its digits — use only a brief color cross-fade (~600ms) on the affected figure; money UI here is calm on purpose, and a rolling-odometer effect would feel more like a game score than an account balance.
8. Keep the navy gradient hero present in dark mode exactly as in light mode — dropping it to a flat dark surface loses the one moment that carries the brand's visual identity most strongly.
9. Use 120-300ms ease-out transitions with no spring/bounce anywhere financial data is involved — segmented-toggle slides, chart-range morphs, and sticky-bar reveals should all read as controlled and precise, matching a 50-year-old brokerage's voice.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Ledgerpoint — a self-directed brokerage app for retail investors"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Accounts list, Account detail (Positions/Balances/Activity), Quote detail, Trade ticket + Review + confirmation]
- Account types supported: [e.g. brokerage, retirement, banking — affects the account-type icon set]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must swap Schwab Blue/Navy for the client's own two-color brand system while keeping the gain/loss discipline]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 16+ baseline]
- Real-time quote/order data source: [state whether a live market-data feed exists or mock data should be used]
- Dark-mode requirement: [full parity required, including the navy hero gradient]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the navy/blue brand pair, light and dark surface steps, the theme-aware gain/loss/flat semantic colors, and a Source Sans 3-style type ramp with a tabular-numerals modifier.
2. Full component code for the Account Hero (navy gradient, Total Value, day-change line) and the Account List Cell (icon chip, name/masked-number, balance/percent-change).
3. The complete Trade Ticket component: Buy/Sell segmented control, tabular field rows, Estimated Cost row, and the sticky Review Order / Place Order button pair, plus a Review screen restating every field read-only.
4. The Balances Tiles 2-column grid and a Positions Table (sortable, tabular, right-aligned columns with a bold total row).
5. Motion and haptic notes: the balance color cross-fade, segmented-toggle slide timing, chart-range morph, and which haptic (light/medium/success) fires at tab change vs. Place Order vs. order-accepted confirmation.
6. A dark-mode pass confirming the navy hero gradient is unchanged, cards get a 1pt border in place of a shadow, and text/surface tokens swap correctly.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver phrasing for an account row and a trade-ticket field, Dynamic Type behavior (total value/titles/body scale; tab labels and ticket field values stay fixed for layout), and confirmation that dark-navy-on-Schwab-Blue and both gain/loss color pairs pass WCAG AA.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Chime Design System
summary: Build Chime's calm, mint-soaked banking UI: a full-bleed mint balance hero, a SpotMe overdraft banner, and instant transaction alerts.
description: Build Chime's calm, mint-soaked banking UI: a full-bleed mint balance hero, a SpotMe overdraft banner, and instant transaction alerts that treat everyday spending as neutral rather than alarming.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Chime's soft off-white/green-charcoal canvas, the Chime Mint gradient, and a DM Sans type ramp with an always-bold, tabular numeral rule
The signature mint Balance Hero card (superscript cents, translucent-dark action buttons, mint-glow shadow) plus the SpotMe banner and Instant Transaction Alert toast
Transaction-row and status-chip specs with the neutral-ink-not-red spending rule, plus motion/haptic notes for a calm, trust-building money app
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer who specializes in consumer neobanking products, with particular skill at translating an emotional design brief ("make banking feel calm and non-punitive") into concrete color rules, component states, and motion timing rather than vague mood language.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is a barely-green off-white #F6FBF8 in light mode and a deep green-charcoal #0E1411 in dark mode — never neutral white or black. Chime Mint (#1EC677 light / #00D67E dark, pressed #16A862) is not a lone accent but the brand's entire personality, applied generously rather than sparingly; a brighter SpotMe Mint (#2EE6A6) is reserved for the fee-free-overdraft feature specifically. Surfaces step to #FFFFFF/#F0F6F2 (light) and #16201B/#1F2C25 (dark) with hairline dividers at #E4EDE8/#243029. Text runs #0F1A14/#5C6E63/#90A399 (light) and #EAF2EC/#9DB0A4/#6B7E72 (dark), with a special near-black mint-tinted "Balance Ink" (#062014) used only on the mint hero card for maximum contrast.
The critical semantic rule: incoming money renders in positive mint (#0FAE63 light / #00D67E dark), but everyday outgoing spending renders in neutral primary-text ink, NOT red — red (#E5484D / #FF6B6B) is reserved exclusively for declined transactions, failed payments, and negative-balance states. Typography is DM Sans (SIL OFL) at friendly weights (400 body, 600 row titles, 700 headers/numbers/buttons, never thin or black); every amount is bold and tabular, and the balance hero renders at 44pt with its cents shrunk to a 26pt superscript.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Chime: (1) the Balance Hero Card — a full-bleed 24pt-radius mint gradient (#1EC677 to #12A862) panel with the giant balance, superscript cents, and two translucent-dark (rgba(6,32,20,0.14)) action buttons sitting inside it, lifted by a mint-tinted glow shadow rather than a gray one; (2) the SpotMe Banner — a fee-free-overdraft feature shown with a star/shield icon chip, a status line, and the available limit rendered in bright mint, treated as a headline trust feature rather than a subtle setting; (3) the Instant Transaction Alert — a push notification plus in-app toast with a solid mint circular check icon firing the instant money moves, reinforcing a real-time trust loop; (4) status chips (Posted/Pending/SpotMe covered/Declined) each with their own tinted pill color; (5) an inline "2 days early" early-direct-deposit badge, explicitly celebrated rather than merely noted; (6) heavily rounded geometry everywhere — 24pt hero, 14pt buttons/fields, pill chips — as the literal expression of the brand's softness.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never color routine outgoing spending red — render it in neutral primary-text ink; red is reserved strictly for declined, failed, or negative-balance states, because coloring everyday purchases red would make ordinary life feel like a string of losses, which directly contradicts the brand's emotional goal.
2. Never use pure white or neutral black for the canvas — light mode is a barely-green off-white #F6FBF8 and dark mode is a green-charcoal #0E1411; both carry a faint mint tint that keeps the brand present even in "neutral" surfaces.
3. Treat mint as the whole personality, not a single accent button — it should appear generously (hero, buttons, chips, icons) rather than being confined to one CTA the way a typical single-accent app would use it.
4. Round everything heavily and consistently — 24pt on the hero, 14pt on buttons/fields/tiles, full pill on chips — because the softness of the geometry is explicitly part of the emotional pitch, not an arbitrary style choice.
5. Never bury the balance — it is deliberately the loudest, largest (44pt/700) element on the home screen, positioned in the top third; competing headline elements above or beside it undercut the core "here's what you can spend" promise.
6. Use the mint-glow shadow (a tinted rgba(30,198,119,...) shadow, not gray) under the balance hero specifically — a generic neutral drop shadow there loses the "lit from within" quality that's called out as this component's signature.
7. Keep every amount bold (weight 700) and tabular, never proportional — this applies uniformly to the balance, transaction amounts, and the SpotMe limit, so money is always instantly scannable.
8. Fire the Instant Transaction Alert (push + in-app toast) the moment money moves, with a solid mint check icon — treat this as a real-time behavior requirement, not just a static toast mockup, since the immediacy is the actual trust mechanism.
9. Keep motion soft — springs with damping ~0.8 and ease-outs, never harsh or snappy easing — and haptics gentle; a jarring animation on a banking app contradicts the calm-and-reassuring brief just as much as a wrong color would.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Haven — a fee-free digital bank account for gig workers"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Home (balance + SpotMe + activity), Move Money, Card, Grow/savings]
- Overdraft/advance feature: [does this app have a SpotMe-equivalent feature to design, or should that section be omitted?]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must substitute the client's own accent color for mint while keeping the neutral-spending / red-only-for-failures color rule]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 16+ baseline, iOS 17+ for .sensoryFeedback on alerts]
- Real transaction data source: [state whether real transaction/deposit data exists or placeholders are needed]
- Dark-mode requirement: [full parity required / nice-to-have]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the off-white/green-charcoal canvas, the full mint scale (brand, bright, pressed, soft-fill, SpotMe), the neutral-vs-positive-vs-negative semantic rule, and a DM Sans-style type ramp.
2. Full component code for the Balance Hero Card (gradient, superscript-cents balance, translucent action buttons, mint-glow shadow) and the Transaction Row (merchant tile, name/meta, tabular amount with the neutral-spending rule applied).
3. The SpotMe Banner and the Instant Transaction Alert toast, including the toast's slide-in/auto-dismiss behavior.
4. The Status Chip component covering all four states (Posted/Pending/SpotMe covered/Declined) with their distinct tint pairs.
5. Motion and haptic notes: balance count-up odometer timing, the alert toast's spring parameters and auto-dismiss window, transaction-row insert animation, and which haptic (soft/medium/light) fires at each event.
6. A dark-mode pass confirming the green-charcoal canvas, softened mint-glow shadow, and full token swap for every component above.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver phrasing for the balance hero and a transaction row (explicitly stating direction — "received" vs "sent" — since color alone can't carry that), Dynamic Type behavior (balance/titles/body scale; tab labels and the superscript-cents ratio stay fixed), and a Reduce Motion fallback for the count-up and alert-slide animations.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Coinbase Design System
summary: Build Coinbase's institutional-clean crypto UI: one electric blue accent, brand-colored asset icons, tabular prices, and the 4-up Buy/Sell/Send/Receive row.
description: Build Coinbase's institutional-clean crypto exchange UI: one electric blue accent, brand-colored asset icons, tabular price columns, and the 4-up Buy/Sell/Send/Receive action row that makes crypto feel like a real exchange.

whatYouGet: SwiftUI Color/Font tokens for Coinbase's white/near-black institutional palette, Coinbase Blue accent, and the Display/Sans/Mono three-way typographic split
Component specs for the Asset Row (brand-colored icon, mini sparkline, tabular price/change), the Portfolio Hero + chart, and the signature 4-up Buy/Sell/Send/Receive action row
Wallet-address and trade-confirmation component specs plus motion/haptic notes for a subtle, low-shadow institutional feel
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS/SwiftUI engineer specializing in institutional-grade fintech and crypto-exchange interfaces, skilled at building information-dense list rows (icon + sparkline + tabular figures) that stay performant and legible, and at applying restrained elevation that reads as "serious exchange" rather than "flat" or "glossy."
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas is white #FFFFFF in light mode and a cool-tinted near-black #0A0B0D in dark mode (deliberately not pure #000, to stay visually tied to the brand blue). Surfaces step to #F7F8FA/#EEF0F3 (light) and #13151A/#1E2026 (dark) with #E1E4E8/#2A2E36 dividers. The single brand accent is Coinbase Blue #0052FF (pressed #0040CC, tint #E5EDFF), used for primary CTAs, the active tab, the C-mark logo, and links — and only there. Each cryptocurrency asset carries its own official brand color for its circular icon: Bitcoin #F7931A, Ethereum #627EEA, USDC #2775CA, Solana #9945FF, Cardano #0033AD, Tether #26A17B — this color diversity across the asset list is treated as a deliberate part of the visual identity, not something to normalize into one accent. Semantic gain/loss: Success Green #05B169, Loss Red #CF202F, each with a tinted pill background (#E6F7EF / #FCE7E9).
Typography splits three ways: Coinbase Display (Inter as substitute) for hero numbers ≥28pt (the 40pt portfolio value, the 56pt Buy/Sell entry amount), Coinbase Sans (Inter) for everything else in the body/list/button layer, and Coinbase Mono (JetBrains Mono) used ONLY for wallet addresses, transaction hashes, and exposed order-book numbers — never for a regular price. Tabular figures are non-negotiable on every financial number. Ticker symbols (BTC, ETH) are tracked wider (+0.3pt) at 13pt, treated as small branded monograms.
Distinctive UI patterns unique to Coinbase: (1) the Asset Row — a 64pt row with a 40pt brand-colored icon circle, a two-line name/ticker-plus-holdings block, an inline 56x20pt mini sparkline colored by 24h direction, and a right-aligned tabular price-plus-change pair; (2) the 4-up action row (Buy/Sell/Send/Receive) at the top of every asset detail screen, four equal-weight cards signaling "this is a full exchange, not a toy"; (3) the Portfolio Hero + chart, an all-caps eyebrow label over a 40pt Display value over a green/red delta, with a full-bleed 2pt line chart (no area fill) whose color can follow the day's direction; (4) the geometric "C" coin-mark logomark, always a perfect circle with a horizontal line, used both as brand lockup and a rotating/pulsing loading indicator; (5) extremely restrained shadow use (0.04-0.08 opacity) versus most consumer fintech, described explicitly as institutional-minimal rather than glossy.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never introduce a second blue for anything — Coinbase Blue #0052FF is the sole brand accent for CTAs, the active tab, and the C-mark; any other "brand-ish" blue in the UI is a mistake, not a variant.
2. Never render an asset's icon in a monochrome or app-accent color — each cryptocurrency keeps its own official brand color (Bitcoin orange, Ethereum purple, USDC blue, etc.); this color diversity across the list is explicitly part of the identity, not noise to tame.
3. Use Coinbase Mono strictly for wallet addresses, transaction hashes, and exposed order-book figures — never for an ordinary price or portfolio value, and never use the Sans/Display faces for an address; this distinction is a hard technical/brand line, not a style preference.
4. Use #0A0B0D (a cool-tinted near-black), not pure #000000, for primary text and the dark canvas — the slight tint is what keeps dark mode feeling tied to the blue brand rather than generic.
5. Enable tabular numerals on every price, percentage, and quantity without exception — the "institutional asset list" feel depends entirely on prices and deltas aligning in a clean column.
6. Keep the 4-up Buy/Sell/Send/Receive action row as four genuinely equal-weight cards with custom icons (up-arrow/down-arrow/paper-plane/QR) — do not shrink it to a single dropdown or button, since its whole purpose is signaling "this exchange supports the full set of real actions."
7. Cap shadow opacity at roughly 0.04-0.08 with short blur radii — anything heavier reads as a different, glossier consumer-fintech brand rather than Coinbase's institutional-minimal elevation language.
8. Never let green mean "falling" or red mean "rising" — color binds strictly to price direction, identically to how a brokerage app would treat it, since this is a financial-trust rule as much as a style rule.
9. Track ticker symbols (BTC, ETH, USDC) at +0.3pt letter-spacing wherever they appear inline — treat them as small branded monograms rather than plain abbreviated text.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name & one-line purpose: [e.g. "Ledger & Co — a retail crypto exchange app for a new regional market"]
- Screens needed: [e.g. Home portfolio + chart, asset list, asset detail with 4-up actions, Buy/Sell amount entry, wallet-address display]
- Assets supported: [e.g. a fixed list of major coins, or a searchable full market — affects list length/sparkline cost]
- Literal clone or inspired-by adaptation: [state clearly]
- Existing brand constraints (if adapting): [e.g. must swap Coinbase Blue for the client's own accent while keeping per-asset brand-color icons and the Mono-for-addresses rule]
- Target iOS version: [e.g. iOS 16+ baseline]
- Real market-data source: [state whether a live price/chart feed exists or mock data should be used]
- Dark-mode requirement: [full parity required / nice-to-have]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI `Color` and `Font` extension file covering the white/near-black canvas, the single Coinbase Blue accent, the per-asset brand-color palette, semantic gain/loss colors, and the Display/Sans/Mono three-tier type ramp with a tabular-numerals modifier.
2. Full component code for the Asset Row (brand-colored icon, two-line text block, inline mini sparkline, tabular trailing price/change) and the Portfolio Hero + full-bleed line chart with range chips.
3. The 4-up Buy/Sell/Send/Receive action row and the Buy/Sell fullscreen amount-entry modal (Display-face hero amount, currency toggle, sticky CTA).
4. The wallet-address display component (Mono face, truncated middle, tap-to-copy toast) and a Trade Confirmation card.
5. Motion and haptic notes: Buy/Sell tap scale-spring, order-confirmation checkmark reveal, chart-scrubber drag behavior, the C-mark's rotation/pulse loading states, and which haptic fires at each step.
6. A dark-mode pass confirming the cool-tinted near-black canvas, brightened dark-mode blue (#3B6CFF) for AA contrast, and that per-asset brand icon colors stay unchanged across themes.
7. An accessibility pass: VoiceOver phrasing for an asset row (name, ticker, holdings, price, direction) and the 4-up action buttons, Dynamic Type behavior (portfolio hero and Buy/Sell amount clamp at a maximum scaled size; wallet addresses and tab labels stay fixed), and confirmation that Coinbase Black-on-white and white-on-blue both pass WCAG AA.
</what_to_give_me>
